extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and students of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for forming and evaluating generalisations and analogical inferences in scientific reasoning, including when generalisation is justified, how probability supports it, and the value of extreme instances and comparisons across conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive reasoning as inverse of deductive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: All inductive reasoning is an inverse application of deductive reasoning and consists in demonstrating that the consequences of certain assumed laws agree with observed facts of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction is founded on the same principle as deduction (the substitution of similars). Induction involves showing that assumed laws yield consequences that match observed data; it is not simply arguing from one particular to another without forming general propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: No inference from particulars to particulars; ascend to general propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no such process as inferring from particulars to particulars; one must ascend to general propositions before deducing particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot safely infer of a particular (e.g., 'Mr. Gladstone must die') from knowledge of other particulars unless a general proposition (e.g., 'all men must die') has been established. The fundamental principle of substitution of similars gives no warrant for asserting that a particular exactly matches others without probability analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use theory of probability to justify generalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the theory of probability (the Inverse Method of Probabilities) to calculate how likely it is that, from a series of similar events, we may infer the recurrence of like events under identical circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When precise data are lacking, one may make rough assumptions (e.g., that similars in some respects are similar in others), but should estimate the probability of beliefs according to the available data to minimise error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of generalisation and analogy (degree-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalisation and analogy differ only by degree: generalisation relies on wide extension and usually little intension; analogy relies on great intension (many points of resemblance) and small extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probability of inference depends on either the number of instances (extension) or the depth of resemblance (intension). What is wanting in extension must be made up by intension, and vice versa. Examples: gravity/inertia association (generalisation); white polar spots on Mars compared to Earth's ice (analogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy inference principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy is founded on the probability that similar things have causes of the same kind and produce the same effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more perfect the similarity in many points, the greater the probability of inferring additional like properties. Kant and Laplace formulations are cited: more points of resemblance imply more further resemblances; use close examination to confirm analogical inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two senses of 'generalisation'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'generalisation' can mean (1) recognising a common nature in even two objects (grouping and strengthening comprehension), and (2) extending from a fact or partial law to many unexamined cases (predictive generalisation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First sense deepens understanding of observed particulars (e.g., grouping rainbow-like colours); second sense predicts unobserved occurrences (e.g., assuming all substances can assume three states based on many trials). Both are important and often linked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of generalisation: gives power over particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalising is worthwhile because it strengthens comprehension of particulars and grants power to apply knowledge broadly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General theories reveal properties unapparent in single cases and allow transfer of insights across domains (e.g., undulatory theory of light inspired by sound; study of conic sections). De Morgan's observation: study of the general enhances power over the particular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare degrees of generality; judge law applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: A key scientific skill is recognising and estimating degrees of generality of properties and judging how far laws are likely to apply in particular circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even absent exact probability calculation, scientists should form judgments in general agreement with probabilistic principles and the data. Training develops a 'tact' for judging applicability (e.g., when crystal-axis effects vs uniform solids, or gases vs liquids/solids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use corresponding conditions when comparing substances
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking general laws across substances, compare them under corresponding conditions (e.g., points equally distant from their boiling points) to reveal underlying generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons at corresponding states can show nearer equality of laws and coefficients (example: different alcohols compared at corresponding temperatures show similar expansion and vapour tensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about inferring across physical states or conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume properties observed in one condition (solid, liquid, gas) hold in another without specific evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ice is an insulator while water conducts electricity; conducting power varies with temperature differently in solids vs liquids. Many apparent differences may be explained when substances are compared under corresponding circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise some laws as nearly universal but remain open to revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain laws (e.g., Newton's laws of motion and universal gravitation) are held to be true of all matter, but they should be subject to experimental scrutiny and revision when discordant observations arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Newton's pendulum experiments and Bessel's repetition; Nicolai's suggestion and subsequent checks. Universal laws ought to be repeatedly tested and confirmed by diverse calculations/observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many properties are variable in degree; beware absolute negations
rubrics_metrics.description: Most qualities vary in degree across substances; properties once thought absent may be present only in very low degrees (e.g., magnetism, conductivity, opacity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tendency undermines rules that declare absolute universals based solely on presence in all tested bodies; Newton's rule about universal qualities is questioned as qualities often vary in degree rather than being strictly absent/present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extreme (ostensive/predominant) instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme or ostensive instances—cases where a property is exhibited in a high degree—are valuable for revealing the nature under investigation and are convenient materials for experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Francis Bacon's 'Ostensive Instances' and examples (quicksilver for density, magnet for attraction, Iceland spar for double refraction) show how striking examples historically guided discovery and subsequent detection of milder instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability of generalisation rests on instances and resemblance depth
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability that a generalisation or analogical inference is true depends on the number of observed instances (extension) and/or the depth (intension) of resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where extension is small, deeper resemblance across many qualities must compensate; where intension is thin, many instances support generality. Use both when possible to strengthen inferences.
